questions.q: Why were all four models run through the same preprocessing pipeline and the same 15 cross-validation splits?
options: Scikit-learn requires identical settings for every model
It makes every model score the same
Only then can differences in score be attributed to the model rather than to the data prep or the luck of the split
It removes the need to look at more than one metric
questions.explain: A fair comparison changes one thing at a time. Identical pipelines and identical folds also make a paired comparison possible.

questions.q: Why use repeated 5-fold cross-validation here instead of a single 5-fold run?
options: With only 454 churners in training, a single run is noisy; repeating gives 15 scores per model and a better sense of spread
Repeated cross-validation trains models faster
Single 5-fold runs cannot compute average precision
It uses the test set as extra validation data
questions.explain: Each validation fold holds about 90 churners, so one split can be lucky or unlucky. Fifteen splits average that out and reveal the spread.

questions.q: The forest's mean AP was 0.328 versus 0.325 for logistic regression, with a fold-to-fold standard deviation around 0.03. What is the right reading?
options: The forest is clearly better and should be shipped
Logistic regression is clearly better
The models are statistically identical to the dummy
The difference is tiny relative to the noise, so treat them as tied and decide on other factors
questions.explain: A gap of 0.003 against a spread of 0.03 is not a finding. Speed, explainability and ease of deployment should help decide.

questions.q: Histogram gradient boosting scored slightly below logistic regression (AP 0.314 vs 0.325). What does this tell you?
options: Gradient boosting never works on tabular data
A more flexible model is not automatically better; with modest signal and good features, simple models can match it
The boosting model must have leaked data
Boosting cannot handle missing values
questions.explain: Extra flexibility only helps if there is structure left to find. Here it did not, though its settings were untuned starting values.

questions.q: Why is the paired comparison (win counts on identical folds) described as a description rather than a p-value?
options: Because win counts are always random
Because the folds overlap in training data, so the 15 scores are not independent
Because paired comparisons only work with regression
Because average precision cannot be compared across models
questions.explain: Cross-validation folds share training rows, so fold scores are correlated. Standard significance tests assume independence and would be overconfident.
